projects.title: Robo-Catcher
projects.question: How do you catch, index, and return a ball without a hand-off?
projects.problem: Close the loop for a solo player: catch the ball, feed it, and return it.
projects.contribution: Feeding subsystem co-lead; machine electronics and firmware.

media.alt: The finished catching and return machine on the field.
media.caption: Field hardware. Photography credit retained in the case-study footer.

media.alt: CAD assembly of the return mechanism.
media.caption: Design view / return mechanism

chapters.label: Catch
chapters.title: Bring the ball into the system.
chapters.summary: The capture structure collects the incoming ball and feeds it toward the indexer. It is the first stage in a machine designed to close the practice loop.
chapters.decision: Capture, feeding, and return were separate team subsystems. The hand-off between them had to work as one system.
chapters.contribution: My scope: feeding, plus the electronics and firmware for the complete machine.

chapters.label: Index
chapters.title: Make the next position repeatable.
chapters.summary: A dual-chamber indexer receives a ball, rotates 180 degrees, and presents it to the return mechanism.
chapters.decision: I modeled the load before choosing the stepper and driver. The case study reports a 1.8x torque safety factor.
chapters.contribution: I co-led the feeding subsystem and programmed its indexing and limit-switch logic.

chapters.label: Return
chapters.title: Complete the loop.
chapters.summary: The return mechanism sends the ball back to the player. The controller coordinates motor drive, feeder indexing, and the wireless interface.
chapters.decision: Emergency cut-offs remove motor power independently of the microcontroller.
chapters.contribution: I owned the machine electronics and firmware, including motor control and safety logic.
